1.pericope_label: So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression. Now the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions in their cities were, the Israelites, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinims.

schools.summary: Delitzsch corrects the division of the sentence against the Greek and Latin versions, which attach the words about Judah to the preceding clause, and rejects the argument that Israel here means only the northern tribes, since the shorter title of the source is admitted by its own proponent to name the same work as the longer ones; he also denies that the next verse is a heading for the list of the city's residents, taking it as introducing the chapter.

Gill cautions that the preceding chapters do not reproduce the register whole, since two tribes are not reckoned there at all and the rest only in part, and identifies the first inhabitants as those who returned on the proclamation of Cyrus to their former possessions.

Clarke describes the four groups named as the whole structure of the nation since the days of Joshua, ending with the Nethinim descended from the Gibeonites, and supposes others taken in war were added later; Wesley reads the general name Israelites as deliberately restoring what belonged to the people before the division of the kingdoms.

Henry reads the first verse as a note on the genealogies just finished, gathered out of a civil record rather than a canonical book, refuses to let the mention of the captivity pass without its lesson — that the judgment be remembered as a warning, and that we own our own transgression when we speak of what has befallen us — and observes that trouble drives together those who have been at variance.

themes: So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression.
Now the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions in their cities were, the Israelites, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinims.

3.pericope_label: And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh; Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the opening clause identical with the parallel and the clause naming Ephraim and Manasseh peculiar to this chapter, treating it as the ordinary freedom of a compiler working from a fuller source rather than as invention, and argues from the length of the interval that neither genealogy can be complete; Delitzsch sets the first name among three chiefs of Judah's principal families and states the divergence without softening it.

Gill notes that Judah and Benjamin furnished the largest numbers both into the captivity and out of it, and records the divergence over the first name in the register, Uthai being called Athaiah elsewhere with a differently reckoned ancestry.

Wesley explains the differences by the Hebrew habit of giving one man several names and by the passage of time between the two returns; Clarke presses the second reason alone, holding that this list gives the company that came with Zerubbabel while the fuller parallel takes in those who followed.

debates.question: Why do the two registers give this family a different ancestry?

positions.position: Each compiler selected different names from a longer roll that held both series; the equivalences that remain are ordinary contractions.
Several names for one man, or different men entirely, since this list gives the first return and the other those who came later.
The divergence is real and is left standing: no ancestor named here appears in the earlier genealogies of Judah.

themes: And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh;
Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah.

5.pericope_label: And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety. And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah,

schools.summary: Delitzsch shows the derivation from Shiloh to be unsuitable in a list of Judah's descendants, restores the form used for Shelah's family elsewhere, and traces the faulty pointing to the fuller spelling of the name; Ellicott reaches the same reading with the support of the Greek and the Targum, but parts from Delitzsch over what the closing number counts, taking it for the total of one clan only where Delitzsch refers it to the heads of all three.
Gill denies that the Shilonites are named from the Ephraimite city, preferring the reading that derives them from Shelah the son of Judah and citing the Targum's rendering, the tribe of Shelah.

debates.question: What does the number six hundred and ninety count?

positions.position: The remaining heads of all three Judahite families, since the plural pronoun reaches back over the three chiefs named.
The Zarhites only, the parallel giving a separate figure for another clan and leaving the third uncounted.

themes: And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons.
And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety.
And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah,

8.pericope_label: And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah; And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six. All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers.

schools.summary: Delitzsch guards the sense of the summary line, which describes the heads named rather than the brethren just numbered; Ellicott identifies two forms of one name within the verse, observes that this house had lived in Jerusalem before the exile as well as after, and reads the parallel's differing figure as following two names run together without a conjunction.
Gill names the three remaining Benjamite houses, notes that none of the men is mentioned elsewhere, and reads the total as the count of Benjamites resident in the city, exceeding that of Judah.

Wesley offers two explanations of the smaller figure in the parallel without choosing between them: that it counts only those whom the lot appointed to the city, this one adding the volunteers, or that some first settled there had since died or moved away.

themes: And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah;
And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six. All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers.

10.pericope_label: And of the priests; Jedaiah, and Jehoiarib, and Jachin, And Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of the house of God;

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the three names at the head of the section are priestly courses rather than persons, and treats the parallel's father-and-son reading as a copyist's error; Delitzsch reads them the same way and identifies the ruler with the Azariah of the earlier genealogy, grandfather of the Jehozadak carried to Babylon.

Gill states simply that these were the priests who returned and settled in the city, and traces the pedigree of the ruler of the house back through Hilkiah and Zadok to Ahitub, identifying him with the Seraiah of the other records.

Clarke distinguishes the office from the high priesthood, which at this time belonged to Jeshua the son of Jozadak: the ruler of the house stood next in authority, with charge of the temple guard and command of the priests and Levites, the officer elsewhere called the second priest.

themes: And of the priests; Jedaiah, and Jehoiarib, and Jachin,
And Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of the house of God;

12.pericope_label: And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer; And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God.

schools.summary: Ellicott reconciles the second house name by name — variants, a probable mistake for a similar name, two forms of one name, and a link that is either an extra generation or an anticipation of the next name — concluding that the two lines are originally identical, and notes the courses involved; on the total he doubts the plain reading altogether, offering three constructions and preferring the one that spreads the number over the whole priestly section.
Gill lists the three links this chapter passes over in the first pedigree, and takes the closing total plainly, as a number exceeding the men of Judah and Benjamin in the city together.

Clarke is staggered rather than satisfied by the total, calling it a prodigious number of ecclesiastics for the service of a single temple and noting that the gatekeepers are not even included in it; Wesley asks why the men are called mighty men of valour and answers that it is a qualification for the office, since a priest might meet real opposition in enforcing the censures and keeping the sacred things secure.

debates.question: What does the figure of one thousand seven hundred and sixty count?

positions.position: The priests, plainly — a total exceeding the laymen of Judah and Benjamin in the city.
Not priestly clans, which would be impossibly many; the number covers all the guilds of the whole priestly section, and the phrase before it has been misplaced.

themes: And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;
And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God.

14.pericope_label: And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph; And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sorts the same men by Levitical descent — Merarite, Gershonite, Merarite again — and notices that the last of them lived out in the villages of the Netophathites rather than in the city.

Gill marks the transition to the third class and sorts the names, tracing one line back to Asaph the singer of David's time and passing on the identifications and alternative forms found in the other registers.

Henry reads the section as evidence of the temper of the returned people, who had smarted for their former neglect of the ordinances and then gone without them, and so began at the right end; he draws two rules from it — that those who cannot yet reach a temple must not be without a tabernacle, God's work never being left undone for want of a place to do it in, and that the allotment of employments followed the model drawn up by David and Samuel, so that a long interruption ended in the ancient landmarks being observed again.

themes: And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;
And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph;
And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites.

17.pericope_label: And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief; Who hitherto waited in the king’s gate eastward: they were porters in the companies of the children of Levi. And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the Lord, were keepers of the entry.

schools.summary: Delitzsch divides the watch among the four named heads, one to each side, observes that the agreement with the parallel register ends at this point, and argues that the words until now presuppose a standing temple and so a pre-exilic source — granting only in general the objection that the gate's old name might have survived; Ellicott takes the names for families or guilds holding the gates by inheritance, proving it from the same warder appearing in David's day and after the exile, moves the clause naming Shallum chief into the following verse, and reads the archaic wording about the camps of Levi as deliberately carrying the temple watch back to the Mosaic sanctuary.

Gill gives the office in a phrase, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle, holds that the porters were set in the same order after the captivity as before, and traces Shallum's descent through Kore to Ebiasaph.

Clarke identifies the king's gate as the one by which the kings of Judah went up, and supplies from Jarchi what the keeping meant in practice: to let no one but the priests approach while the sacred service was being performed.

debates.question: Does the phrase until now date the source before or after the exile?

positions.position: Before: the words presuppose the temple standing when the register was drawn up.
The question does not arise as posed, since the warder is a guild rather than a man, and the gate would keep its old name in the restored temple.

themes: And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;
Who hitherto waited in the king’s gate eastward: they were porters in the companies of the children of Levi.

And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the Lord, were keepers of the entry.

20.pericope_label: And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the ruler over them in time past, and the Lord was with him. And Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office.

schools.summary: Delitzsch defines the office rather than the identity, Phinehas holding it while his father was high priest, and refuses to read the words about the Lord's presence as a statement of fact, taking them for a blessing tied to the covenant of peace; on Zechariah he notes the missing conjunction and the real difficulty of the verse, identifies the man with the firstborn of Meshelemiah under David, and admits he can give no definite answer why this one name is singled out; Ellicott agrees on the period and observes that the verse turns abruptly back from the age of Moses to the age of David.

Gill takes Phinehas for the son of Eleazar who served in the days of Moses, noting that Kimchi mentions others who made him a different Levite of the same name, places Zechariah after the captivity rather than in David's time, and reads the total as a figure fixed under David below which the number might not fall.

debates.question: To which age does the porter Zechariah belong?

positions.position: David's — he is the firstborn of Meshelemiah who drew the northern watch by lot.
Rather the time after the captivity, in an office David had established and whose order was still kept.

themes: And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the ruler over them in time past, and the Lord was with him.
And Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.

All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office.

23.pericope_label: So they and their children had the oversight of the gates of the house of the Lord, namely, the house of the tabernacle, by wards. In four quarters were the porters, toward the east, west, north, and south. And their brethren, which were in their villages, were to come after seven days from time to time with them.

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains the phrase house of the tabernacle as a precaution against confining the house of the Lord to Solomon's temple, sets the keepers to the four quarters by David's arrangement, and reads the seventh day as the sabbath on which each class took its turn, the chiefs they joined being the resident four; Ellicott gives the plain reason for the same phrase, that the temple was not built in David's day, and traces the four-sided watch from the tent of meeting to the temple's square enclosure.
Gill draws the hereditary character of the office from these verses — those appointed under David were succeeded by their posterity — and cites the Targum for twenty-four wards in all.

Wesley dates the oversight from David, distinguishes the tabernacle meant from the tent David pitched for the ark, and describes the changeover from the incoming side: the courses were exchanged every seventh day and the new men stayed until the next sabbath, serving with the chief porters who never left.

themes: So they and their children had the oversight of the gates of the house of the Lord, namely, the house of the tabernacle, by wards.
In four quarters were the porters, toward the east, west, north, and south.
And their brethren, which were in their villages, were to come after seven days from time to time with them.

26.pericope_label: For these Levites, the four chief porters, were in their set office, and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God. And they lodged round about the house of God, because the charge was upon them, and the opening thereof every morning pertained to them.

schools.summary: Delitzsch adds the charge of the chambers and treasuries to their watch, gives the verse's own reason for their lodging round the house, and draws attention to the key being in their keeping, so that the opening of the doors each morning was theirs; Ellicott renders the opening clause as describing them in fixed position or trust, the four heroes of the warders, contrasts the chiefs abiding in the temple with the members settled in the villages at pastoral work, and moves the clause about chambers and treasuries into the following verse.

Gill distinguishes the four chief gatekeepers from the rest — they stood over the whole body, were never rotated into the country villages, and remained on the spot superintending the others — and places their lodging in chambers against the outer wall so that they were at hand for their office.

themes: For these Levites, the four chief porters, were in their set office, and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God.
And they lodged round about the house of God, because the charge was upon them, and the opening thereof every morning pertained to them.

28.pericope_label: And certain of them had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale. Some of them also were appointed to oversee the vessels, and all the instruments of the sanctuary, and the fine flour, and the wine, and the oil, and the frankincense, and the spices. And some of the sons of the priests made the ointment of the spices.

schools.summary: Delitzsch separates the costly vessels fetched briefly from the treasure-chamber and counted out and back from the general charge of the vessels in daily use and of the stores the service consumed, and identifies the ointment as the holy anointing oil, which is why its making belonged to the priests; Ellicott marks the same division of duties and says outright what the tallying was for, that nothing should be taken.

Gill describes the traffic in vessels from the priests' side, the Levites carrying them to the priests for the sacrifice and returning them to their places afterwards, notes that the standing charge included delivering things out as occasion arose and seeing them returned, and states the limit the Levites could not cross, that the care of the spices did not extend to compounding the ointment.
Clarke puts the restriction at its full weight: none but the priests were permitted to make that ointment, and everyone else was forbidden it on pain of death.

themes: And certain of them had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale.
Some of them also were appointed to oversee the vessels, and all the instruments of the sanctuary, and the fine flour, and the wine, and the oil, and the frankincense, and the spices.
And some of the sons of the priests made the ointment of the spices.

31.pericope_label: And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans. And other of their brethren, of the sons of the Kohathites, were over the shewbread, to prepare it every sabbath.

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the man set over the pan-baking as the firstborn of the Korahite already named among the gatekeepers, notices that calling him one of the Levites deliberately contrasts with the sons of the priests just before, and can only compare the unique word for what was baked with the term for a sheet-iron pan; he assigns the shewbread to certain Kohathites and ties their brethren back to the Korahite house, the bread having to be laid fresh every sabbath; Ellicott renders the office as fixed charge over the making of the pancakes and observes that the narrative has turned back from priestly duties to Levitical ones.

Gill supplies the working detail of the shewbread — twelve loaves set out weekly and the old ones removed, the Levites making the bread but the priests setting it on the table — and notes the named family that held the office under the second temple.

themes: And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans.
And other of their brethren, of the sons of the Kohathites, were over the shewbread, to prepare it every sabbath.

33.pericope_label: And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night. These chief fathers of the Levites were chief throughout their generations; these dwelt at Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads both verses as subscriptions closing the Levitical section rather than fresh entries, noting that the list opened with the singer families and closes by naming them again; he works at the obscure description of their freedom, adopting the sense Rashi and Kimchi gave it, immunity from other duties, and warns that the phrase day and night states the reason rather than a literal round of hours; Ellicott agrees that the words point back to the men already treated and gives a more literal rendering of the second subscription.
Gill describes the singers as masters of the song who presided in that part of the worship, and takes the closing subscription to cover everyone named in the chapter so far.

themes: And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night.
These chief fathers of the Levites were chief throughout their generations; these dwelt at Jerusalem.

35.pericope_label: And in Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, whose wife’s name was Maachah: And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab,

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the repeated register as deliberate and structural, given again to join the history of the kingship to the genealogies and to introduce the account of Saul's death, and argues from the differences between the two copies that this one was taken from a separate and better preserved document; Ellicott takes up the names themselves, hearing the divine title Rock in one and noting that two have been run together into a single name.
Gill points out that the name of Gibeon's father is supplied here where the earlier list left it out.

Clarke finds a departure by the translators rather than the copyists: the word rendered wife is in the original the word for sister, though the ancient versions, the parallel passage and almost all the early editions read wife.

Henry states the duplication without softening it and then says what he suspects — that it arose from a copyist whose eye caught the same words in the earlier chapter and carried on with what followed there, and who, seeing his mistake, was unwilling to spoil his page — closing with the maxim that what is redundant does no harm.

debates.question: Why does the Saul genealogy appear a second time?

positions.position: By design, to connect the genealogies with the history of the kingship that follows; the differences show a separate and better source.
Probably by a transcriber's slip, the scribe's eye catching identical words in the earlier chapter.

outliers.claim: That the repetition is most likely a copyist's error left uncorrected rather than part of the design of the book — a suggestion Henry makes only after granting that the originals of these books contain some errors of transcription.

themes: And in Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, whose wife’s name was Maachah:
And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab,
